claim: A 2.6 Å resolution single particle cryo-EM reconstruction of rotavirus VP6 was determined from movies recorded with a total exposure of 100 electrons/Å².
source: Using a 2.6 Å resolution single particle cryo-EM reconstruction of rotavirus VP6, determined from movies recorded with a total exposure of 100 electrons/Å2, we obtained accurate measurements of optimal exposure values over a wide range of resolutions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution achieved and the total exposure used in the study.

claim: Measured optimal exposure values at low and intermediate resolutions are considerably higher than those obtained previously for crystalline specimens.
source: At low and intermediate resolutions, our measured values are considerably higher than obtained previously for crystalline specimens, indicating that both images and movies should be collected with higher exposures than are generally used.
evidence: The abstract compares measured values to previous crystalline specimen studies.

claim: Images and movies should be collected with higher exposures than are generally used.
source: At low and intermediate resolutions, our measured values are considerably higher than obtained previously for crystalline specimens, indicating that both images and movies should be collected with higher exposures than are generally used.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the comparison of measured optimal exposure values.

claim: A method of using optimal exposure values to filter movie frames yields images with improved contrast that lead to higher resolution reconstructions.
source: We demonstrate a method of using our optimal exposure values to filter movie frames, yielding images with improved contrast that lead to higher resolution reconstructions.
evidence: The abstract describes a demonstrated method and its outcomes.

claim: The 'high-exposure' technique should benefit cryo-EM work on all types of samples, especially those of relatively low-molecular mass.
source: This 'high-exposure' technique should benefit cryo-EM work on all types of samples, especially those of relatively low-molecular mass.
evidence: This is a prediction about the applicability of the technique based on the study results.

claim: Electron microscopy of biological specimens has recently led to a number of structures determined at near-atomic resolution.
source: Electron microscopy of isolated macromolecules and their complexes (single particles) embedded in a thin layer of vitreous ice (cryo-EM) has recently led to a number of structures determined at near-atomic resolution (Liao et al., 2013; Allegretti et al., 2014; Bartesaghi et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014), a level of detail that had previously been restricted to X-ray crystallography and NMR (for a recent review of the technique, see Cheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Near-atomic resolution detail had previously been restricted to X-ray crystallography and NMR.
source: Electron microscopy of isolated macromolecules and their complexes (single particles) embedded in a thin layer of vitreous ice (cryo-EM) has recently led to a number of structures determined at near-atomic resolution (Liao et al., 2013; Allegretti et al., 2014; Bartesaghi et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014), a level of detail that had previously been restricted to X-ray crystallography and NMR (for a recent review of the technique, see Cheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical state of structural biology methods, supported by citation.

claim: Radiation damage is a limiting factor in the resolution of EM images of biological specimens.
source: A limiting factor in the resolution of EM images of biological specimens is radiation damage because the imaging of such specimens ultimately relies on the interaction of electrons with the sample.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in electron microscopy.

claim: Some electron-specimen interactions result in energy being deposited in the specimen, causing radiation damage.
source: Some of these interactions will result in energy being deposited in the specimen, and these will cause radiation damage (Glaeser, 1971; Henderson, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work on radiation damage.

claim: Radiation damage fundamentally limits the information present in images because the useful signal added per incident electron decreases with increasing electron exposure, while the added noise remains approximately constant.
source: The radiation damage fundamentally limits the information present in the images because the useful signal added per incident electron decreases with increasing electron exposure, while the added noise (image contrast originating from other parts of the sample as well as inelastic scattering) remains approximately constant.
evidence: This describes the fundamental mechanism by which radiation damage limits information.

claim: An optimal exposure can be chosen that will maximize the signal-to-noise ratio at a given resolution if the signal gain per unit exposure is known.
source: If the signal gain per unit exposure is known at a given resolution, an optimal exposure can be chosen that will maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at that resolution (Hayward and Glaeser, 1979; Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This principle is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The rate of exposure-dependent signal decay has been measured by following the intensities of fading diffraction spots in exposure series obtained from 2D and thin 3D crystals.
source: The rate of exposure-dependent signal decay has been measured by following the intensities of the fading diffraction spots in exposure series obtained from 2D and thin 3D crystals (Unwin and Henderson, 1975; Hayward and Glaeser, 1979; Stark et al., 1996; Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Higher resolution intensities tend to fade faster than lower resolution intensities in crystalline specimens.
source: These studies demonstrated that higher resolution intensities tend to fade faster than lower resolution intensities, and that the rate of fading for all resolutions is slowed under liquid nitrogen conditions relative to room temperature conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies on crystalline specimens.

claim: The rate of fading for all resolutions is slowed under liquid nitrogen conditions relative to room temperature conditions.
source: These studies demonstrated that higher resolution intensities tend to fade faster than lower resolution intensities, and that the rate of fading for all resolutions is slowed under liquid nitrogen conditions relative to room temperature conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies on crystalline specimens.

claim: The fading of diffraction spots can be described by an exponential decay characterized by Ne, the resolution-dependent critical exposure after which spot intensities are reduced to 1/e of their starting values.
source: The fading of the spots can be described by an exponential decay that is characterized by Ne, the resolution-dependent critical exposure after which spot intensities are reduced to 1/e of their starting values.
evidence: This describes the mathematical model used to characterize radiation damage.

claim: A plot of ln(SNR(k)) vs N should have a slope of -1/Ne(k).
source: We can see from Equation 1 that a plot of ln(SNR(k)) vs N should have a slope of −1/Ne(k), and Baker et al. (2010) demonstrated that this relationship is true not just in the case of measurements of instantaneous signal, but also in the case of a detector that integrates measured intensities over time.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of Equation 1, validated by citation.

claim: The relationship between ln(SNR(k)) and N is true for both instantaneous signal measurements and detectors that integrate measured intensities over time.
source: We can see from Equation 1 that a plot of ln(SNR(k)) vs N should have a slope of −1/Ne(k), and Baker et al. (2010) demonstrated that this relationship is true not just in the case of measurements of instantaneous signal, but also in the case of a detector that integrates measured intensities over time.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al. (2010).

claim: The signal present in crystal diffraction spots is maximized at an optimal exposure of approximately 2.5 times the critical exposure.
source: Hayward and Glaeser (1979) showed that the signal present in crystal diffraction spots is maximized at an optimal exposure of ∼2.5 times the critical exposure.
evidence: This is a finding from Hayward and Glaeser (1979).

claim: It is typically better to slightly overexpose a specimen than slightly underexpose.
source: The SNR increase per unit exposure is larger below the optimal exposure than the corresponding rate of SNR decay beyond the optimal exposure; thus, it is typically better to slightly overexpose a specimen than slightly underexpose.
evidence: This is an inference from the asymmetric behavior of SNR around the optimal exposure.

claim: An exposure of 2.5 Ne is expected to optimize the signal in images at a given resolution.
source: An exposure of 2.5 Ne is also expected to optimize the signal in images at a given resolution due to the analogy between image and crystal data as explained above.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analogy between images and crystal diffraction data.

claim: Direct measurement of the critical exposure on non-crystalline specimens has proven difficult in the past for a number of reasons.
source: Despite studies of the general effects of radiation damage on single-particle specimens (Conway et al., 1993), direct measurement of the critical exposure on non-crystalline specimens has proven difficult in the past for a number of reasons.

source: Firstly, recording a series of images with increasing exposure would have led to images with SNRs so low that they would be difficult to analyze.

claim: Until recently, the resolutions commonly obtained with the single-particle method were of insufficient quality to follow radiation damage at near-atomic resolution.
source: Secondly, until recently the resolutions commonly obtained with the single-particle method were of insufficient quality to follow radiation damage at near-atomic resolution (better than 4 Å).
